name: California YIMBY Education Fund (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: renters and homeowners in California, through the extra homes state housing laws allow.
summary: The California YIMBY Education Fund is the tax-deductible 501(c)(3) arm of California YIMBY, a 501(c)(4) that lobbies for state laws letting more homes be built in California; the Education Fund does the research, public education, organising and coalition work behind the same campaign ($3.05 million spent in 2024, the latest filed year; gifts to the 501(c)(4) aren't deductible). Both organisations' average real spending over 2017-2024 is counted against the Education Fund's share of their part in the state housing laws of those years: the ADU clean-up laws that followed the 2016 reforms (about 11,000 extra backyard homes a year), and a judged 2,500 extra homes a year from streamlining, parking and other laws. Each extra home is valued on the site's log-consumption scale at California prices: its rent above what it costs to build, kept by whoever builds it, and the fall in rents it brings, which renters gain and better-off landlords lose (a little over half the value). With the next dollar at 42% of the average, it comes to about 0.13 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, about twice the median of the site's global-health models. The result is mostly uncertainty: the resources others put into the same laws, how much rents fall per extra home and the share of the ADU boom due to the later laws are judgments, and the model's own ranges span several thousandfold; both branches are discounted for missing data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: California YIMBY Education Fund

sections.title: Cost

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The extra homes a year the period's state housing laws bring, from the state's permit counts and our judgment of the laws' part in them.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What an extra home is worth: the rent above its building cost to whoever builds it, and the fall in rents for every renter, each at its receivers' consumption on the site's log scale, over the home's discounted life.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share

source.title: California Department of Housing and Community Development, Housing Element Annual Progress Report table A2 (data.ca.gov, resource fe505d9b-8c36-42ba-ba30-08bc4f34e022), ADU rows: building permits and certificates of occupancy by year

rows.explainer: The cities' Annual Progress Report count for 2024, the same series as the completion share below (so permits and completions are counted alike). HCD's handbook gives a lower 30,354 for 2024 (Between 2016-2024, the number of ADUs permitted annually in the state grew from 1,336 to 30,354, HCD ADU Handbook, March 2026), the low end; the high end allows for under-reporting, about 5% above.

rows.label: Share of 2024's ADU permits due to the ADU laws of 2017-2024 (rather than the 2016 laws alone)
rows.explainer: California YIMBY was founded after the 2016 laws (SB 1069, AB 2299) that started the boom, so only the follow-on laws count: AB 68 and AB 881 (2019, which removed local zoning barriers), AB 2221 (2022), AB 976 (2023, no owner-occupancy rules), SB 1211 and AB 3057 (2024) and the other clean-up bills its retrospective lists. Under the 2016 rules permits reached 15,086 in 2019 (APR table A2, data.ca.gov); after the 2019 package took effect they rose to 24,640 in 2021 and 39,077 in 2024 in the same series. Part of that rise is the 2016 framework maturing (permits had grown 67% from 2018 to 2019), part the follow-on laws: 45%, from 25% to 65%. Its own report argues it took the clean-up bills to iron out the framework.

rows.label: Share of permitted ADUs that are built

source.title: California Department of Housing and Community Development, Housing Element Annual Progress Report table A2 (data.ca.gov, resource fe505d9b-8c36-42ba-ba30-08bc4f34e022), ADU rows: building permits and certificates of occupancy by year
source.page: SUM(NO_BUILDING_PERMITS) and SUM(NO_OTHER_FORMS_OF_READINESS) by YEAR where UNIT_CAT = 'ADU'

rows.explainer: Completions (certificates of occupancy) in a year over the previous year's permits ran 0.57 to 0.67 in 2020-2025, and 2025's completions over the average of 2023-2024 permits 0.65; 2023's over 2021's permits 0.75. Some permits lapse and some completions go unreported. 65%, from 57% to 75%.

rows.label: Extra ADUs built a year because of the 2017-2024 ADU laws
Extra homes built a year because of the period's other state housing laws
rows.explainer: The other laws the two organisations sponsored, co-sponsored or backed in 2017-2024: streamlined approval (SB 35 in 2017, extended and widened by SB 423 in 2023), parking reform near transit (AB 2097, 2022, which it co-sponsored), housing on commercial land (AB 2011), lot splits and duplexes (SB 9), faith-based housing (SB 4), and stronger housing-element enforcement. Use has been uneven: SB 35 drew about 18,000 proposed homes in 2018-2021 (Terner Center), about 4,500 a year, mostly subsidised affordable homes some of which would have been approved another way; SB 9 approvals ran at 310 to 977 units a year in 2023-2025 (APR table A); YIMBY Law found AB 2011 used by 2 projects in 2023 and 8 in 2024 and SB 4 by none. Net of homes that would have been built anyway: 2,500 a year, from 700 to 7,000.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention in the year
rows.explainer: No casework: the organisations change state law.

rows.label: Median gross rent, California, 2020-2024 (US$ a month)

source.title: US Census Bureau, QuickFacts, California (American Community Survey 2020-2024)

rows.explainer: The typical rent in California, the base for both the rents an extra home earns and the fall in rents it brings.

rows.label: Owner-occupied housing unit rate, California, 2020-2024

source.title: US Census Bureau, QuickFacts, California (American Community Survey 2020-2024)

rows.explainer: The same five-year series as the median rent. census.gov refuses automated fetches; the figure is QuickFacts' as indexed by search.

rows.label: Share of California's occupied homes that are rented
rows.explainer: The rest are owner-occupied: a fall in rents moves money from landlords to renters only on rented homes.

rows.label: An ADU's rent against the median rent
rows.explainer: ADUs are small (most are under 1,000 square feet, many converted garages) but often in high-rent neighbourhoods; most new ADUs in the costliest suburbs are reported affordable to households under 80% of the area's median income (California YIMBY's retrospective, from HCD's data). 0.85 of the median, from 0.65 to 1.05.

rows.label: Other laws: share of a new apartment's rent above what it costs to build, land included (the regulatory gap)
rows.explainer: Glaeser and Gyourko find median house prices more than double the minimum profitable cost of building (land at an unregulated price included) in Los Angeles, Oxnard-Ventura and San Francisco-Oakland (2.84 in San Francisco), and 1.25 to 2 in San Diego: a gap of 20% to 65% of the price, mostly bid-up land, which they read as a regulatory tax. A home that rules no longer block is worth its rent and costs less to build, and the difference is the economy's gain. 50%, from 30% to 65%.

rows.label: ADU laws: share of an ADU's rent above what it costs to build
rows.explainer: An ADU builder buys no land, so its gap is rent against construction cost alone. The statewide ADU owner survey found a median construction cost of $150,000 ($250 a square foot; 37% under $100,000, 71% under $200,000), about $184,000 in 2024 prices (the survey asked about ADUs built through 2019; US consumer prices rose about 23% from 2019 to 2024). At the ADU rent here (about $20,800 a year) and a user cost of about 6.5% a year (interest, upkeep, depreciation), the median ADU leaves about 42% of its rent; one costing $250,000 about 22%, a $100,000 garage conversion about 69%. 40%, from 20% to 60%.

source.title: UC Berkeley Center for Community Innovation and Terner Center, Implementing the Backyard Revolution: Perspectives of California's ADU Owners (April 2021)
source.quote: median statewide construction cost of an ADU of $150,000, or $250/square foot

rows.label: Fall in rents (%) for each 1% more homes in the state
rows.explainer: Across US metros, Pew's analysis of Zillow data (July 2025) finds each 10% more housing from 2017 to 2023 went with rents growing about 5% less to 2024: 0.5 per 1%, for a market open to people moving in from nearby, and correlational. A whole state is less open than a metro, so its rents fall more; the Reserve Bank of Australia's model of a national market uses 2.5% lower housing costs for each 1% more dwellings (RBA Research Discussion Paper 2019-01), the high end (the paper's Abelson et al. figure, 3.6%, is house prices, not rents, and isn't used). 1, from 0.4 to 2.5.

source.title: Pew Charitable Trusts, New Housing Slows Rent Growth Most for Older, More Affordable Units (31 July 2025)
source.quote: every 10% increase in a market's housing supply from 2017 to 2023 correlated with rents growing 5% less

rows.label: California's consumption per person in dollars, against the US average
rows.explainer: California's prices run about 12% above the US average (the Bureau of Economic Analysis's regional price parities, about 112 for California), so the same living standard takes more dollars there and a dollar counts for less on the log scale. 1.12, from 1 to 1.25.

rows.label: Consumption of homeowners who build ADUs, as a multiple of the US survey average per person
rows.explainer: ADUs are built by homeowners with a lot and the money to build, better off than homeowners as a whole: per person, US homeowners spend 1.06 times the survey average ($90,117 a household of 2.6) and the top income fifth 1.44 times ($150,342 for 3.2), against $78,535 for 2.4 (Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024 via FRED, series CXUTOTALEXPLB0106M, CXU980010LB0106M, CXUTOTALEXPLB1702M, CXU980010LB1702M). 1.25, from 1.06 to 1.6.

rows.label: Consumption of landlords and developers, as a multiple of the US survey average per person
rows.explainer: Rental housing is owned by better-off households, funds and firms; developers and landowners keep the gain on new apartments. Around the top income fifth and above it: 2 times the survey average per person, from 1.2 to 3.5, as the phone companies' owners in Prison Policy Initiative's model are judged at 2 (1 to 4).

rows.label: Renters' consumption per person (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The shared survey spending per person (the base the site uses for the people a programme serves, docs/normalization.md 2.14), scaled to renters by the survey's own renter figures (per household, turned into per person with the shared household sizes), and to California's price level.

rows.label: ADU builders' consumption per person (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The same survey base (rule 2.14 keeps the national accounts for everyone's consumption, as taxpayers'; ADU builders are a group), times the multiple and California's price level.

rows.label: Landlords' and developers' consumption per person (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: As above, for landlords and developers.

rows.label: Rent saved by California's renters a year for each extra home (US$)
rows.explainer: One home more in a stock of Q lowers rents by rent_fall_per_stock/Q; the saving on the renters' Q × renter_share homes is rent_fall_per_stock × renter_share × the yearly rent, whatever Q is. It comes out of landlords' rents.

rows.label: Renters' gain less landlords' loss, per extra home a year (units of value)
rows.explainer: On the site's log scale a small change in consumption is worth the dollars over consumption per person (spread over a household, household size cancels): the renters' gain less the same dollars to the better-off landlords.

rows.label: Gain to the owner who builds an ADU, a year (units of value)
rows.explainer: The ADU's rent above what it costs to build, kept by the homeowner who builds it (or saved by the family member who lives in it), at the homeowner's consumption.

rows.label: Gain to the developer or landowner who builds an apartment, a year (units of value)
rows.explainer: The home's rent above its cost of building, kept by whoever builds and owns it, at landlords' consumption.

rows.label: Share of the extra homes a year that the market would have built later anyway
rows.explainer: Once a law would have come (after the years a win counts, below), builders would partly catch up on the homes it brought earlier; the extra homes' lead shrinks at this rate from then on. A separate question from whether the law would have come: that is the years a win counts. 5% a year, from 2% to 15%.

rows.label: Years a new home lasts
rows.explainer: Wood-frame homes and converted garages in California last decades; 50 years, from 30 to 80. Discounted, the later years count little.

rows.label: Years from a home's completion until the catch-up starts
rows.explainer: The homes are built over the years a win counts; the average one is finished halfway through, and the counterfactual law (and the catch-up) arrives at the end of those years: half of them later.

rows.label: Discounted years an extra home counts
rows.formula: pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, catch_up_start_years) + (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - catch_up_start_years) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate + catch_up_rate, home_life_years - catch_up_start_years)
rows.explainer: Each extra home's yearly gain over its life, discounted at the shared rate, with the catch-up shrinking its lead only once the law would have come.

rows.label: Chance a year that a won housing law is repealed, overturned or gutted
rows.explainer: State housing laws face local ballot initiatives to restore local control (Our Neighborhood Voices tried in 2022 and 2024), lawsuits by charter cities (against SB 9) and local ordinances that blunt them (YIMBY Law counted 140 against SB 9). Most of the period's laws still stand, and the shared electoral-reform repeal rate is 3% (1-8%). 2% a year, from 0.5% to 6%. Homes already built stay built: it shortens only the years of extra building.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: ADU laws: years from the law until the extra homes are lived in
rows.explainer: Laws take effect the January after they pass; an ADU takes months to permit and a year or so to build. 1.5 years, from 1 to 2.5.

rows.label: Other laws: years from the law until the extra homes are lived in
rows.explainer: Apartment projects take a year or two to approve and finance and two years to build. 3 years, from 2 to 5.

rows.label: ADU laws: discounted years of extra building
rows.explainer: The years a won reform counts, discounted at the shared rate plus the repeal rate, after the wait.

rows.label: Other laws: discounted years of extra building
rows.explainer: As for the ADU laws.

rows.label: ADU laws: value per campaign year, before adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: Extra homes a year, each worth its builder's gain and the renters' net gain over its discounted life, for the discounted years the laws count, spread over the eight campaign years.

rows.label: Other laws: value per campaign year, before adjustments (units of value)
rows.explainer: As for the ADU laws.

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per person affected per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Zero: the homes' good is valued in money on the log scale above, which would count it twice.

rows.label: Health gained per person affected per year (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Zero here: less homelessness from lower rents is a side-effect row (ue_homelessness); crowding isn't counted.

rows.label: Income gained per person affected per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: Zero: the branches are valued per home and per dollar above.

rows.label: Probability the win happens because of this work
rows.explainer: Every law counted is in force; the organisations' part in them is their share of the coalitions' resources (the attribution below), one question, not two.

rows.label: Years from the win until it takes effect
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the win takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate (for reading; each branch discounts its own wait).

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: For reading; each branch has its own.

rows.label: Years of freedom gained per person released
rows.explainer: No casework.

rows.label: Wellbeing gained per year of freedom (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: No casework.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person released, discounted
ADU laws: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The permits are cities' own reports, which HCD doesn't verify, and the laws' effect is read from the timing of the boom, not a controlled study; Elmendorf and Nall (2024) and planning research agree the state's rules caused it. The valuation (the regulatory gap, the fall in rents) rests on market studies, not on these homes. 0.8, from 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: Other laws: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The homes these laws added are our judgment from counts of applications and uses, with no study of what would have been built without them. 0.7, from 0.5 to 0.9.

rows.label: ADU laws: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the homes the 2016 rules would have brought anyway are taken out in adu_followon_share, and that the laws would have come some day is in the years a win counts (Convention 5).

rows.label: Other laws: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the homes count is net of those that would have been built anyway, and the laws' coming some day is in the years a win counts.

rows.label: Both organisations' real spending over 2017-2024 (2024 dollars)
rows.explainer: The eight years' spending above, in 2024 prices: the organisations' side of the coalitions.

rows.label: ADU laws: share of both organisations' spending that went on ADU work
rows.explainer: California YIMBY supported the clean-up bills (AB 68 and AB 881, AB 2221, AB 976, SB 1211, Wikipedia), sponsored AB 3057 (2024) and published the ADU retrospective, among a dozen or more bills a year. 15%, from 8% to 30%.

rows.label: Casita Coalition's total expenses, 2021-2024 (US$)

source.title: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, Casita Coalition (EIN 84-3860605), filings by year; 2024 from its Form 990 e-file (IRS TEOS, scripts/irs-990.py)

rows.explainer: The coalition of ADU builders and advocates formed in 2020, whose whole work is ADU law and practice: all of its spending counts (128,114 + 220,041 + 324,916 + 535,635).

rows.label: ADU laws: the large lobbies' and groups' spending on them, 2017-2024 (US$)
rows.explainer: The California Association of Realtors, the building industry, Habitat for Humanity California, regional business groups and local YIMBY groups lobbied for the clean-up bills among many others. Cal-Access reports each lobbying employer's payments in total, not by bill, and its pages refuse automated fetches, so the ADU part is a judgment: First Tuesday reports over $43 million a year of the realtors' state and national dues counted as lobbying expenses (an older figure), and a dozen ADU bills among the hundreds each lobby tracks over four sessions take a small share. $12 million, from $3 million to $40 million.

rows.label: ADU laws: legislators' and HCD's staff time on them, 2017-2024 (US$)
rows.explainer: About a dozen bills, each with an author's office and two policy committees in each house (several staff-months a bill at a few hundred thousand dollars a staff-year with overheads), plus HCD's ADU handbook, technical assistance and review letters to cities over the period. $20 million, from $5 million to $50 million.

rows.label: ADU laws: everyone else's resources behind the follow-on laws, 2017-2024 (US$)

rows.label: Side effect: higher productivity of other workers as California's job centres grow
rows.explainer: The movers' own higher wages are mostly paid back in the rents that the builders' gain above already counts; what is new is the spillover to other workers when a city grows (urban productivity rises by about 2% to 5% for each doubling of density, the agglomeration literature, Combes and Gobillon's 2015 review). The aggregate gains are disputed: Hsieh and Moretti (2019) put the cost of housing limits in the most productive cities at 36% of US growth from 1964 to 2009, Glaeser and Gyourko (this model's source) at about 2% of GDP at most, and a 2026 comment by Greaney far less. 3% of the modelled value, from 0 to 15%.

rows.label: Side effect: less homelessness from lower rents
rows.explainer: Homelessness across US regions tracks rents far more than poverty or addiction (Colburn and Aldern, Homelessness Is a Housing Problem, 2022; Byrne et al. 2013). At the fall in rents above, an extra home lowers rents by about a ten-millionth, which with California's roughly 187,000 homeless people and a rent elasticity of homelessness near 1 is about 0.02 fewer homeless people per home-year; at a homeless person's excess deaths and life-satisfaction gap that is about 2% of a home-year's value here. 2%, from 0.5% to 6%.

rows.label: Side effect: costs to neighbours (construction, parking, crowding of services)
rows.explainer: Neighbours bear construction noise and more competition for parking and services; studies of new buildings find nearby rents fall rather than rise, so displacement is not counted as a harm. -3%, from -10% to 0.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The three side effects, each a row above, applied to both branches; lower emissions are counted in tonnes through the climate bridge below.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO2e a year an extra home in California saves against where its household would otherwise live
rows.explainer: Coastal California households emit less than almost anywhere in the US: a mild climate, a cleaner grid and shorter drives in infill places (Glaeser and Kahn, The greenness of cities, Journal of Urban Economics 2010, find San Diego and San Francisco the lowest-emitting US metros; the CoolClimate household footprints of Jones and Kammen vary by several tonnes between places). Against living inland or in a hotter, car-bound state: 2 tonnes a home-year, from 0.5 to 4.
